Whether "the soul is the same as the body" or "the soul is one thing and the body another," whether "a Tathāgata exists after death," or "a Tathāgata does not exist after death," or "a Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death," or "a Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death";
Whatever view there is of such a kind— a state of views, a thicket of views, a wilderness of views, a distortion of views, a vacillation of views, a fetter of views,
a seizing, a settling upon, an adherence, a misapprehension, a wrong path, a false course, falsity, a sectarian standpoint, a perverted grasping— this is what is meant by "wrong view."
This is called adherence to views.
All wrong view is adherence to views.
These phenomena are adherences.
Which phenomena are not perversions?

With the exception of those [perversion] phenomena, all remaining wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena belonging to the sense-sphere, the fine-material sphere, the immaterial sphere, and the unincluded [supramundane];
the aggregate of feeling …pe… the aggregate of consciousness.
All form and the unconditioned element—these phenomena are not misapprehensions.
2.3.2.9.2. The Dyad of Misapprehended Phenomena.
Which phenomena are adhered to?
Wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena that are subject to taints, belonging to the sense sphere, the fine-material sphere, and the immaterial sphere;
the aggregate of form …pe… the aggregate of consciousness.
These phenomena are misapprehended.
Which phenomena are not misapprehended?
Those that are not included [within the mundane], namely the paths, the fruits of the paths, and the unconditioned element.
These phenomena are not subject to misapprehension.
2.3.2.9.3. The Dyad of Factors Associated with Misapprehension:
Which phenomena are associated with misapprehension?
Those phenomena associated with those [ten] corruptions— the aggregate of feeling …pe… the aggregate of consciousness—
these phenomena are associated with corruptions.
Which phenomena are dissociated from corruptions?
Those phenomena dissociated from those [corresponding] states— the aggregate of feeling …pe… the aggregate of consciousness;
all form, and the unconditioned element—
these phenomena are dissociated from the underlying tendency to misapprehension.
2.3.2.9.4. The Dyad of Grasping and Grasped At Which phenomena are both grasping and grasped at?
That very same grasping is both grasping and grasped at.
Which phenomena are both adhered to and not themselves adherence?

With the exception of those phenomena which are adhered to by those [other] phenomena, all remaining phenomena associated with the taints (*sāsrava*)—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate; belonging to the sense-sphere, the fine-material sphere, or the immaterial sphere;
namely, the aggregate of form …pe… the aggregate of consciousness.
These phenomena are both objects of misapprehension and not themselves misapprehensions.
2.3.2.9.5. The Dyad of Phenomena Disjoined from Misapprehension but Objects of Misapprehension:
Which phenomena are disjoined from misapprehension yet are objects of misapprehension?

Those states which are dissociated from those [defilements], yet are associated with the taints (āsava)—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate; whether belonging to the sense sphere, the fine-material sphere, or the immaterial sphere;
namely, the aggregate of form …pe… the aggregate of consciousness—these states are dissociated from misapprehension but are objects of misapprehension.
Which phenomena are dissociated from the perversions and are not adhered to?
The supramundane paths, the fruits of the paths, and the unconditioned element—
these phenomena are dissociated from the perversions and are not adhered to.
Sārammaṇaduka Which phenomena have an object?
The aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness—
these phenomena have an object.
Which phenomena are without an object?
All form and the unconditioned element—these phenomena are without an object.
2.3.2.10.2. The Dyad of Consciousness.
Which states are consciousness?
Eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, the mind-element, and the mind-consciousness-element—
these states are consciousness.
Which phenomena are not mind?
The aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, all form, and the unconditioned element—
these phenomena are not mind.
2.3.2.10.3. The Dyad of Mental Factors (Cetasikaduka) Which phenomena are mental factors?
The aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, and the aggregate of formations.
These states are mental factors.
Which states are non-mental factors?
Consciousness, all matter, and the unconditioned element.
These states are non-mental factors.
2.3.2.10.4. The Couple of States Associated with Consciousness:
Which states are associated with consciousness?
The aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, and the aggregate of mental formations—
these phenomena are associated with the mind.
Which phenomena are dissociated from the mind?
All form and the unconditioned element—
these phenomena are dissociated from consciousness. Consciousness itself should not be said [to be either associated or dissociated].
Associated with consciousness, as well as dissociated from consciousness.
2.3.2.10.5. The Dyad of Conjoined with Consciousness:
Which phenomena are conjoined with consciousness?
The aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, and the aggregate of mental formations—
these phenomena are associated with the mind.
Which phenomena are dissociated from the mind?
All form and the unconditioned element—
these phenomena are dissociated from consciousness. Consciousness itself should not be said [to be either associated or dissociated].
They are associated with consciousness, and they are dissociated from consciousness.
2.3.2.10.6. The Dyad of Originating from Consciousness:
Which phenomena originate from consciousness?
The aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations;
bodily intimation, verbal intimation;
or whatever other matter there is that is mind-born, mind-caused, and mind-originated, such as the sphere of visible form.
The sense-sphere of sound, the sense-sphere of odor, the sense-sphere of flavor, the sense-sphere of the tangible, the space element, the water element,
lightness of form, malleability of form, wieldiness of form, integration of form, continuity of form, and edible food— these phenomena are mind-originated.
Which phenomena are not mind-originated?
Consciousness itself, the remaining material form, and the unconditioned element—
these phenomena are not mind-originated.
2.3.2.10.7. Cittasahabhūduka.
Which phenomena are co-existent with consciousness?
The aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, bodily intimation, and vocal intimation.
These phenomena are co-existent with consciousness.
Which phenomena are not co-existent with consciousness?
Consciousness itself, the remaining materiality, and the unconditioned element.
These phenomena do not coexist with the mind.
2.3.2.10.8. The Dyad of Phenomena that Follow the Mind:
Which phenomena follow the mind?
The aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of volitional formations, bodily intimation, and verbal intimation—
these phenomena are concomitants of the mind.
Which phenomena are not concomitants of the mind?
Mind and the remaining matter, and the unconditioned element—these phenomena do not follow the mind.
2.3.2.10.9. The Dyad of Conjoined and Produced by Mind.
Which phenomena are conjoined with and originated by the mind?
The aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, and the aggregate of mental formations—
these phenomena are conjoined with and originated by the mind.
Which phenomena are not conjoined with and not produced by consciousness?
Consciousness itself, all material form, and the unconditioned element—
these phenomena are not conjoined with and not produced by consciousness.
2.3.2.10.10. The Dyad of Mental Conjoined, Originated, and Coexistent Factors.
Which phenomena are mental conjoined, originated, and coexistent?
The aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, and the aggregate of mental formations.
These phenomena are conjoined with, originated by, and co-existent with the mind.
Which phenomena are not conjoined with, originated by, and co-existent with the mind?
The mind itself, all form, and the unconditioned element.
These phenomena are not conjoined with, originated by, and co-existent with the mind.
2.3.2.10.11. The Dyad of Phenomena Conjoined with, Originated by, and Following the Mind:
Which phenomena are conjoined with, originated by, and following the mind?
The aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, and the aggregate of mental formations—
these phenomena are conjoined with the mind, co-arisen with the mind, and follow along with the mind.
Which phenomena are not conjoined with the mind, do not co-arise with the mind, and do not follow along with the mind?
Mind, all form, and the unconditioned element—these phenomena are not conjoined with, produced by, or concomitant with mind.
2.3.2.10.12. Internal Dyads.
Which phenomena are internal?
The eye-base …pe… the mind-base—
these phenomena are internal.
Which phenomena are external?
The sense-sphere of visible forms …pe… the sense-sphere of mental phenomena—
these phenomena are external.
Which phenomena are clinging?
The eye-base … [and so on] … edible food.
These phenomena are derived.
Which phenomena are not derived?
The aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of volitional formations, the aggregate of consciousness, the four great elements, and the unconditioned element.
These phenomena are not acquired.
2.3.2.10.14. The Dyad of the Acquired:
Which phenomena are acquired?
The results of wholesome and unwholesome states accompanied by taints, belonging to the sense sphere, the fine-material sphere, and the immaterial sphere:
the aggregate of feeling …pe… the aggregate of consciousness;
and that form which arises from action having been performed.
These phenomena are acquired.
Which phenomena are unacquired?
Wholesome and unwholesome phenomena associated with the taints that belong to the sense sphere, the fine-material sphere, and the immaterial sphere.
The aggregate of feeling …pe… the aggregate of consciousness;

those states which are functional (kiriyā), neither wholesome nor unwholesome and not the result of kamma; that form which does not arise from the performance of kamma; the [states] not included [in the mundane sphere], namely the paths, the fruits of the paths, and the unconditioned element—these states are not clung-to (anupādinnā).
2.3.2.11. Group on Clinging (Upādāna-gocchaka) 2.3.2.11.1.
The Dyad on Clinging (Upādāna-duka) Which phenomena are clinging?
There are four kinds of clinging:
clinging to sensual pleasures, clinging to views, clinging to rules and observances, and clinging to a doctrine of self.
In this context, what is clinging to sensual pleasures?

Whatever desire for sensual pleasures, lust for sensual pleasures, delight in sensual pleasures, craving for sensual pleasures, affection for sensual pleasures, fever for sensual pleasures, infatuation with sensual pleasures, and clinging to sensual pleasures—
this is called clinging to sensual pleasures (*kāmupādāna*).
In this context, what is clinging to views (*diṭṭhupādāna*)?
"There is no gift, there is no sacrifice, there is no oblation; there is no fruit or result of deeds well done or ill done;
there is no this world, there is no other world; there is no mother, there is no father;

there are no beings who are reborn spontaneously; there are in the world no ascetics or brahmins who have attained rightly and practiced rightly, who have realized this world and [the world beyond] for themselves by direct knowledge."

And the view, the state of view, the thicket of view, the wilderness of view, the distortion of view, the vacillation of view, the fetter of view, the grasping, the settling upon grasping, the adherence, the misapprehension, the wrong path, the false course, the state of error, [expressed as]: "Having realized the other world for oneself through direct higher knowledge, one declares it"—such a view as this... [is what is meant].
Adherence to a sectarian standpoint and grasping at perversity—
this is called clinging to views (*diṭṭhupādāna*).
With the exception of clinging to rules and observances (*sīlabbatupādāna*) and clinging to a self-theory (*attavādupādāna*), all wrong view is clinging to views.
In this context, what is clinging to rules and observances (*sīlabbatupādāna*)?

It is the view, the course of view, the thicket of view, the wilderness of view, the distortion of view, the vacillation of view, held by those ascetics and brahmins outside this [teaching], who hold that purification comes through virtue, purification comes through observance, or purification comes through both virtue and observance. This is what is called clinging to rules and observances.
The fetter of views, grasping, fixation, adherence, misapprehension, the wrong path, the false course, falsity,
the basis for sectarianism, and the grasping of perversion—
this is called the clinging to rules and observances.
In this context, what is the clinging to a doctrine of self?
Here, an uninstructed worldling—unseeing of the noble ones, unskilled in the Dhamma of the noble ones, undisciplined in the Dhamma of the noble ones;
unseeing of true persons, unskilled in the Dhamma of true persons, undisciplined in the Dhamma of true persons—regards form as self...
He does not regard form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as being in self, or self as being in form.
[He does not regard] feeling … perception … [in the same way].
One regards volitional formations as self... consciousness as self, or self as possessing consciousness, or consciousness as in self, or self as in consciousness.
Whatever view there is of this kind—this resort to views, this thicket of views, this wilderness of views, this distortion of views, this vacillation of views—[is called identity view].
The fetter of views, grasping, settling upon, adherence, misapprehension, the wrong path, the false course, error,
the basis for sectarianism, and the grasping of perversion—
this is called the clinging to a doctrine of self.
These phenomena are clinging.
Which phenomena are not clinging?

With the exception of those phenomena, all remaining wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena belonging to the sense sphere, the fine-material sphere, the immaterial sphere, and the unincluded [supramundane] realm.
The aggregate of feeling …pe… the aggregate of consciousness;
all form and the unconditioned element—
these phenomena are not objects of clinging.
2.3.2.11.2. The Pair on Subject to Clinging (Upādāniyaduka):
Which phenomena are subject to clinging?
They are the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena associated with the taints (āsava), belonging to the sense-sphere, the fine-material sphere, and the immaterial sphere.
The aggregate of form …pe… the aggregate of consciousness—
these phenomena are subject to clinging.
Which phenomena are not subject to clinging?
The paths that are not included [within the mundane], the fruits of the paths, and the unconditioned element—these phenomena are not associated with clinging.
2.3.2.11.3. The Dyad of Factors Associated with Clinging.
Which states are associated with clinging?
Those states which are associated with those [states of] clinging— the aggregate of feeling …pe… the aggregate of consciousness—
these states are associated with clinging.
Which phenomena are dissociated from clinging?
Those phenomena dissociated from those [states of clinging] are the aggregate of feeling …pe… the aggregate of consciousness;
all form, and the unconditioned element.
These phenomena are dissociated from clinging.
2.3.2.11.4. The Dyad of Clinging and the Objects of Clinging:
Which phenomena are both clinging and objects of clinging?
Those very same clingings are both clinging and objects of clinging. Which phenomena are objects of clinging but are not themselves clinging?

With the exception of those phenomena which are objects of clinging, all remaining phenomena associated with the taints (*sāsrava*)—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate—that belong to the sense sphere, the fine-material sphere, and the immaterial sphere.
The aggregate of form …pe… the aggregate of consciousness—these states are both subject to clinging and not themselves clinging.
2.3.2.11.5. The Dyad of Clinging and States Associated with Clinging.
Which phenomena are both clinging and associated with clinging?

The clinging to views is both clinging and associated with clinging through the clinging to sense pleasures; the clinging to sense pleasures is both clinging and associated with clinging through the clinging to views;
the clinging to rules and observances is both clinging and associated with clinging through the clinging to sense pleasures.
Sensual clinging is both clinging and associated with clinging by way of clinging to rules and observances;

clinging to a doctrine of self is both clinging and associated with clinging by way of sensual clinging; and sensual clinging is both clinging and associated with clinging by way of clinging to a doctrine of self.
These states are both clinging and associated with clinging.
Which states are associated with clinging but are not themselves clinging?
Those states which are associated with those [states of] clinging, excluding those states themselves—the aggregate of feeling …pe… the aggregate of consciousness.
These phenomena are associated with clinging but are not themselves clinging.
2.3.2.11.6. The Dyad of Phenomena Dissociated from Clinging but Subject to Clinging:
Which phenomena are dissociated from clinging but subject to clinging?

Those states which are dissociated from those [aforementioned] states— whether they be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate, and whether they belong to the sense sphere, the fine-material sphere, or the immaterial sphere; namely,
the aggregate of form …pe… the aggregate of consciousness—
these states are associated with clinging but dissociated from clinging.
Which phenomena are dissociated from clinging and not subject to clinging?
The states that are not included [within the mundane], the paths and the fruits of the paths, and the unconditioned element—
these phenomena are dissociated from clinging and not subject to clinging.
The second recitation section in the Chapter on Depositions.
2.3.2.12. The Group on Defilements (Kilesagocchaka). 2.3.2.12.1.
The Dyad on Defilements (Kilesaduka).
Which phenomena are defilements?
The ten bases of defilement:
greed, hatred, delusion, conceit, wrong view, doubt, sloth, restlessness, lack of moral shame, and lack of moral dread.
In this context, what is greed? It is lust, infatuation,
compliance, compliance with desire, delight, the lust of delight, infatuation of the mind, longing, infatuation,
cleaving, grasping, intense grasping, attachment, the mire, agitation, deceit, the mother, the progenitor, the seamstress, the netter, the stream, and the state of being stuck.

The thread, the spreading, the extension, the second [craving], the wish, the conduit to existence, the forest, the thicket, the intimacy, the affection, the regard, the bond, the hope, the longing, the state of longing,
the hope for forms, the hope for sounds, the hope for odors, the hope for tastes, the hope for tangibles, the hope for gain, the hope for wealth,
the hope for sons, the hope for life, the muttering, the muttering aloud, the intense muttering, the muttering, the act of muttering, the state of having muttered, and greed.
Lustful longing, the state of being lustfully longed for, the habit of hankering, the desire for excellence, unrighteous passion, improper greed,
attachment, yearning, aspiration, seeking, striving, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, craving for non-existence,
craving for form, craving for the formless, craving for cessation, craving for forms, craving for sounds, craving for odors, craving for tastes, craving for tactile objects.
Craving for existence is a flood, a bond, a tie, clinging, an obstruction, a hindrance,
a covering, a fetter, an affliction, a latent tendency, an obsession, a creeper, a snare, the root of suffering, the source of suffering, the origin of suffering,
Māra’s snare, Māra’s net, Māra’s domain, the river of craving, the web of craving, the whirlpool of craving, the ocean of craving, covetousness, greed, and a root of unwholesomeness.
This is called greed (*lobha*). In this context, what is hatred (*dosa*)?

"He has done me harm"—thus resentment arises; "He is doing me harm"—thus resentment arises; "He will do me harm"—thus resentment arises; "He has done harm to one who is dear and pleasing to me"... [and so on] ...he is doing harm... [and so on].

“‘He will act for my disadvantage’—thus resentment arises; ‘He has acted for the disadvantage of one who is unpleasant and disagreeable to me’ … [and so on] … ‘He is acting for his disadvantage’ … [and so on] … ‘He will act for his disadvantage’—thus resentment arises;
or else resentment arises without cause.”
Whatever such resentment, hostility, antipathy, opposition, anger, provocation, intense provocation, hatred, malice, intense malice, corruption of the mind,
mental corruption, wrath, being wrathful, state of being wrathful, hatred, hating, state of hating, corruption, being corrupted, state of being corrupted, opposition,
counter-opposition, ferocity, or abruptness of the mind— this is called ill will (*vyāpāda*).
Discontent of mind—
this is called hatred.
In this context, what is delusion?
Ignorance regarding suffering; ignorance regarding the origin of suffering; ignorance regarding the cessation of suffering; ignorance regarding the practice leading to the cessation of suffering;
ignorance regarding the past; ignorance regarding the future; ignorance regarding both the past and the future;
and ignorance regarding specific conditionality and dependently arisen phenomena.
Whatever such lack of knowledge, non-seeing, non-comprehension, non-awakening, non-enlightenment, non-penetration, non-grasping,
non-exploration, non-regard, non-reflection, lack of direct experience, dullness, childishness, lack of clear comprehension, delusion, confusion,
total bewilderment, ignorance, the flood of ignorance, the yoke of ignorance, the underlying tendency of ignorance, and the obsession of ignorance— this is what is meant by ignorance.
Delusion, which is the cloak of ignorance and an unwholesome root—
this is called delusion.
In this context, what is conceit?
The conceit "I am superior," the conceit "I am equal," and the conceit "I am inferior";
whatever such conceit there is, whatever ideation, state of being conceited, loftiness, haughtiness, banner, grasping, or desire for self-display of the mind—
this is called conceit (*māna*).
In this context, what is view?

It is the view that "the world is eternal," or "the world is non-eternal," or "the world is finite," or "the world is infinite," or "the soul and the body are the same," or "the soul and the body are different," or "a Tathāgata exists after death."

Or, "The Tathāgata exists after death," or "The Tathāgata does not exist after death," or "The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death," or "The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death"—
whatever view such as this may be, that state of views, that thicket of views, that wilderness of views, that distortion of views, that vacillation of views.
The fetter of views, grasping, fixation, adherence, misapprehension, the wrong path, the false course, falsity,
the basis for sectarianism, and the grasping of perversion—
this is called view.
All wrong view is *diṭṭhi*.
In this context, what is doubt (*vicikicchā*)?
One is hesitant and doubts regarding the Teacher; one is hesitant and doubts regarding the Dhamma; one is hesitant and doubts regarding the Saṅgha.
He is doubtful and uncertain about the training; he is doubtful and uncertain about the past; he is doubtful and uncertain about the future;
he is doubtful and uncertain about both the past and the future; he is doubtful and uncertain about specific conditionality and dependently arisen phenomena.

Whatever kind of doubt, doubting, state of having doubted, perplexity, uncertainty, vacillation, bifurcation, path of two ways, hesitation, holding to various sides, sliding back and forth, lack of penetration, rigidity of mind, mental scarifying— this is called doubt (*vicikicchā*).
In this context, what is sloth (*thina*)?

That which is the mind’s lack of pliancy, lack of serviceability, sluggishness, lingering, sloth, the state of sloth, the state of being slothful, torpor, the state of torpor, the state of being torpid of the mind—
this is called *thina*. In this context,
what is *uddhacca* (restlessness)?
That which is agitation of the mind, lack of tranquility, mental distraction, and instability of the mind—
this is called restlessness.
In this context, what is shamelessness (*ahirika*)?
That which does not feel shame where one ought to feel shame— that which does not feel shame regarding the undertaking of evil, unwholesome states—
this is called moral shamelessness (*ahirika*).
In this context, what is lack of moral dread (*anottappa*)?
That which is not being afraid when one ought to be afraid; that which is not being afraid of the attainment of evil, unwholesome states—this is called lack of moral dread (*anottappa*).
These states are defilements (*kilesa*).
Which phenomena are not defilements?

With the exception of those [defiled] phenomena, all remaining wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena belonging to the sense sphere, the fine-material sphere, the immaterial sphere, and the unincluded [supramundane];
the aggregate of feeling …pe… the aggregate of consciousness.
All form and the unconditioned element—these phenomena are not defilements.
2.3.2.12.2. The Dyad of Defiled Phenomena.
Which phenomena are subject to defilement?
They are the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena associated with the taints, belonging to the sense-sphere, the fine-material sphere, and the immaterial sphere;
namely, the aggregate of form …pe… the aggregate of consciousness.
These phenomena are subject to defilement.
Which phenomena are not subject to defilement?
Those that are not included within the mundane realms—the paths, the fruits of the paths, and the unconditioned element.
These phenomena are untainted.
2.3.2.12.3. The Dyad of the Tainted:
Which phenomena are tainted?
The three unwholesome roots—greed, hatred, and delusion;

the defilements associated with them; the aggregate of feeling associated with them …pe… the aggregate of consciousness associated with them; and the bodily action, verbal action, and mental action originated by them.
These states are defiled.
Which states are undefiled?
Wholesome and indeterminate states belonging to the sense sphere, the fine-material sphere, the immaterial sphere, and those that are not included [within the three realms].
The aggregate of feeling …pe… the aggregate of consciousness;
all form, and the unconditioned element—
these phenomena are undefiled.
2.3.2.12.4. The Dyad of States Associated with Defilements (Kilesasampayuttaduka) Which states are associated with defilements?
Those states which are associated with those [defiled] states—the aggregate of feeling …pe… the aggregate of consciousness.
These states are associated with defilements.
Which states are dissociated from defilements?
Those states which are dissociated from those [defiled] states: the aggregate of feeling …pe… the aggregate of consciousness.
All form and the unconditioned element—these phenomena are dissociated from the defilements.
2.3.2.12.5. The Dyad of Defilement and Corrupt by Defilement.
Which phenomena are both defilements and subject to defilement?
Those very defilements are both defilements and subject to defilement.
Which phenomena are subject to defilement but are not themselves defilements?

Setting aside those phenomena which are defilements, the remaining phenomena associated with the taints (*āsava*)—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate—that belong to the sense-sphere, the fine-material sphere, or the immaterial sphere;
namely, the aggregate of form …pe… the aggregate of consciousness:
these phenomena are both subject to defilement and yet are not themselves defilements.
2.3.2.12.6. The Dyad of Defiled by the Defilements (Kilesasaṅkiliṭṭhaduka) Which phenomena are both defilements and defiled?
Those very defilements are both defilements and defiled.
Which phenomena are both defiled and yet not themselves defilements?
Those phenomena which are defiled by those [defilements], excluding those very phenomena themselves—the aggregate of feeling …pe… the aggregate of consciousness:
these phenomena are both defiled and yet not themselves defilements.
2.3.2.12.7. The Dyad of Defilements and Factors Associated with Defilements Which phenomena are both defilements and associated with defilements?
Greed, together with delusion, is both a defilement and associated with a defilement; delusion, together with greed, is both a defilement and associated with a defilement.
And hatred is a defilement through delusion and is associated with defilement; delusion is a defilement through hatred and is associated with defilement;
conceit is a defilement through delusion and is associated with defilement; delusion is a defilement through conceit and is associated with defilement;
view is a defilement through delusion and is associated with defilement; delusion is a defilement through view and is associated with defilement.
And doubt is both a defilement through association with delusion and associated with defilements; delusion is both a defilement through association with doubt and associated with defilements;
sloth is both a defilement through association with delusion and associated with defilements; delusion is both a defilement through association with sloth and associated with defilements;
restlessness is both a defilement through association with delusion and associated with defilements.
Delusion, through restlessness, is both a defilement and associated with a defilement; moral shamelessness, through delusion, is both a defilement and associated with a defilement;
delusion, through moral shamelessness, is both a defilement and associated with a defilement; lack of moral dread, through delusion, is both a defilement and associated with a defilement;
and delusion, through lack of moral dread, is both a defilement and associated with a defilement.
Greed, together with restlessness, is both a defilement and associated with defilement; restlessness, together with greed, is both a defilement and associated with defilement.
Hatred, together with restlessness, is both a defilement and associated with defilement; restlessness, together with hatred, is both a defilement and associated with defilement.
Delusion, together with restlessness, is both a defilement and associated with defilement; restlessness, together with delusion, is both a defilement and associated with defilement.
Pride, together with restlessness, is both a defilement and associated with a defilement; restlessness, together with pride, is both a defilement and associated with a defilement;
wrong view, together with restlessness, is both a defilement and associated with a defilement; restlessness, together with wrong view, is both a defilement and associated with a defilement;
doubt, together with restlessness, is both a defilement and associated with a defilement; [and] restlessness...
Doubt is both a defilement and associated with defilements; sloth is both a defilement and associated with restlessness;
restlessness is both a defilement and associated with sloth; moral shamelessness is both a defilement and associated with restlessness;
restlessness is both a defilement and associated with moral shamelessness; and moral recklessness...
Restlessness is both a defilement and associated with defilements; restlessness is both a defilement and associated with non-shame.
Greed is both a defilement and associated with defilements; non-shame is both a defilement and associated with greed.
Hatred is both a defilement and associated with defilements; non-shame is both a defilement and associated with hatred.
Delusion, together with moral shamelessness, is both a defilement and associated with defilements; moral shamelessness, together with delusion, is both a defilement and associated with defilements.
Conceit, together with moral shamelessness, is both a defilement and associated with defilements; moral shamelessness, together with conceit, is both a defilement and associated with defilements.

Wrong view, together with moral shamelessness, is both a defilement and associated with defilements; moral shamelessness, together with wrong view, is both a defilement and associated with defilements.
Doubt, together with moral shamelessness, is both a defilement and associated with defilements; moral shamelessness, together with doubt, is both a defilement and associated with defilements;
sloth, together with moral shamelessness, is both a defilement and associated with defilements;
moral shamelessness, together with sloth, is both a defilement and associated with defilements; restlessness, together with moral shamelessness, is both a defilement and associated with defilements.
Shamelessness is both a defilement and associated with defilements through restlessness; lack of moral dread is both a defilement and associated with defilements through shamelessness;
shamelessness is both a defilement and associated with defilements through lack of moral dread.
Greed is both a defilement and associated with defilements through lack of moral dread; lack of moral dread is both a defilement and [associated with defilements] through greed.
It is associated with defilements: hatred is both a defilement and associated with defilements through lack of moral dread;
lack of moral dread is both a defilement and associated with defilements through hatred; delusion is both a defilement and associated with defilements through lack of moral dread;
lack of moral dread is both a defilement and associated with defilements through delusion; conceit is both a defilement and [associated with defilements] through lack of moral dread.
That which is associated with defilements: lack of moral dread is both a defilement and associated with the defilement of conceit;
view is both a defilement and associated with the defilement of lack of moral dread; lack of moral dread is both a defilement and associated with the defilement of view;
doubt is both a defilement and associated with the defilement of lack of moral dread; lack of moral dread is a defilement [associated] with doubt.
And restlessness is both a defilement and associated with defilements; restlessness is both a defilement and associated with defilements through lack of moral dread;
lack of moral dread is both a defilement and associated with defilements through restlessness;

lack of moral dread is both a defilement and associated with defilements through lack of moral dread; and shamelessness is both a defilement and associated with defilements through lack of moral dread.
And [those states] associated with defilements; lack of moral dread is both a defilement and associated with defilements—these states are both defilements and associated with defilements.
Which states are associated with defilements but are not themselves defilements?

With the exception of those states which are associated with those [defilements], the aggregate of feeling …pe… the aggregate of consciousness—these states are associated with defilements but are not themselves defilements.
2.3.2.12.8. The Dyad of States Dissociated from Defilements but Corruptible (Kilesavippayutta-saṅkilesika-duka)
Which phenomena are dissociated from the defilements yet subject to defilement?

Those phenomena dissociated from those [defilements] which are with taints (sāsava), whether wholesome or indeterminate, belonging to the sense-sphere, the fine-material sphere, or the immaterial sphere:
the aggregate of form …pe… the aggregate of consciousness.
These states are dissociated from the defilements yet subject to defilement.
Which states are dissociated from the defilements and not subject to defilement?
The supramundane paths, the fruits of the paths, and the unconditioned element.
These states are dissociated from the defilements and are non-defiled.

2.3.2.13.2. The Pair on What is to be Abandoned by Cultivation.
Which phenomena are to be abandoned by cultivation?

The remaining greed, hatred, and delusion; the defilements associated with them; the aggregate of feeling associated with them …pe… the aggregate of consciousness associated with them; and the bodily, verbal, and mental actions originating from them—these phenomena are to be abandoned by cultivation.
Which phenomena are not to be abandoned by cultivation?

With the exception of those [nine] phenomena, all remaining wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena belonging to the sense sphere, the fine-material sphere, the immaterial sphere, and the unincluded [supramundane];
the aggregate of feeling …pe… the aggregate of consciousness.
All form and the unconditioned element—these phenomena are not to be abandoned by cultivation.
2.3.2.13.3. The Dyad of Roots to be Abandoned by Seeing.
Which phenomena have roots that are to be abandoned by vision?
Three fetters:
personality-belief, doubt, and adherence to rules and observances.
In this regard, what is the view of a personal body (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*)?
Here, an uninstructed worldling—unseeing of the noble ones, unskilled in the Dhamma of the noble ones, undisciplined in the Dhamma of the noble ones;
unseeing of true persons, unskilled in the Dhamma of true persons, undisciplined in the Dhamma of true persons—regards form as self...
he does not regard [it thus]: "the self possesses form," or "form is in the self," or "the self is in form. [He does not regard it thus with respect to] feeling...
perception... [and so on].
One regards volitional formations as self, or self as possessing volitional formations, or volitional formations as being in self, or self as being in volitional formations.

Whatever view there is of this kind, whatever course of views... [and so on] ...whatever perversion and grasping—this is called the "view of self. [The same applies to] consciousness... whatever perversion and grasping—this is called the "view of self."
This is called the view of a personal body (sakkāyadiṭṭhi).
In this context, what is doubt (vicikicchā)?
It is to be perplexed and doubtful regarding the Teacher... [and so on] ...it is the state of being paralyzed and the mental distress of the mind.
This is called doubt (*vicikicchā*).
In this context, what is adherence to rules and observances (*sīlabbataparāmāsa*)?
It is the view held by recluses and brahmins outside of this [teaching]: "Purification comes through rules, purification comes through observances, purification comes through rules and observances."
Any such view, a state of viewing, ... [as previously described] ...
a perverted grasp—this is called adherence to rules and observances (*sīlabbataparāmāsa*).

These three fetters, along with the defilements associated with them, the aggregate of feeling associated with them, ... [and so on] ... the aggregate of consciousness associated with them, and the bodily action, verbal action, and mental action originating from them—[these constitute the category of clinging].
These states have roots that are to be abandoned by vision.
There are three fetters:
personality-belief, doubt, and adherence to rules and observances.
These states are to be abandoned by vision.
The greed, hatred, and delusion associated with them—
these states are the causes to be abandoned by vision.

The defilements associated with that [state], the aggregate of feeling associated with it …pe… the aggregate of consciousness associated with it, and the bodily action, verbal action, and mental action originating from it—
these phenomena have roots to be abandoned by vision.
Which phenomena do not have roots to be abandoned by vision?

Excluding those states, the remaining wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate states belonging to the sense sphere, the fine-material sphere, the immaterial sphere, and the unincluded [supramundane];
the aggregate of feeling …pe… the aggregate of consciousness;
all form, and the unconditioned element—these are the states that are not included in the clinging-aggregates.
These phenomena do not have roots that are to be abandoned by vision.
2.3.2.13.4. The Dyad of Phenomena with Roots to be Abandoned by Cultivation:
Which phenomena have roots that are to be abandoned by cultivation?
The remaining greed, hatred, and delusion—
these states have roots that are to be abandoned by cultivation.

Also included are the defilements associated with them, the aggregate of feeling associated with them …pe… the aggregate of consciousness associated with them, and the bodily, verbal, and mental actions originating from them.
These phenomena have roots that are to be abandoned by cultivation.
Which phenomena do not have roots that are to be abandoned by cultivation?

With the exception of those phenomena, all remaining wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena belonging to the sense sphere, the fine-material sphere, the immaterial sphere, and the unincluded [supramundane] realm.
The aggregate of feeling …pe… the aggregate of consciousness;
all form, and the unconditioned element—
these phenomena have roots that are not to be abandoned by cultivation.
2.3.2.13.5. The Dyad of With-Initial-Mental-Conception (Savitakkaduka) Which phenomena are with initial mental conception?

In the plane of with-initial-mental-conception—the sense-sphere, the fine-material sphere, and the unincluded—excluding initial mental conception itself, the aggregate of feeling associated with it …pe… the aggregate of consciousness.
These states are with initial application (*savitakka*).
Which states are without initial application (*avitakka*)?
Those in the plane without initial application: in the sense-sphere, the fine-material sphere, the immaterial sphere, and the unincluded (unconditioned).
The aggregate of feeling …pe… the aggregate of consciousness;
applied thought, all form, and the unconditioned element—
these phenomena are without applied thought.
2.3.2.13.6. The Pair on With-Reflection (Savicāraduka) Which phenomena are with reflection?

In the plane with reflection—namely, in the sense-sphere, the fine-material sphere, and the unincluded (transcendent)—excluding reflection itself, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness associated with it.
These phenomena are accompanied by sustained application (*savicāra*).
Which phenomena are without sustained application (*avicāra*)?

Those belonging to the plane without sustained application: those of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*), the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*), the immaterial sphere (*arūpāvacara*), and the unconditioned (*apariyāpanna*).
The aggregate of feeling … [and so on] … the aggregate of consciousness;
sustained thought, all form, and the unconditioned element—
these phenomena are without sustained thought.
2.3.2.13.7. The Pair on With Rapture (Sappītikaduka) Which phenomena are with rapture?

In the plane with rapture—namely, in the sense-sphere, the fine-material sphere, and the unincluded (apariyāpanna)—with the exception of rapture itself, the aggregate of feeling associated therewith …pe… the aggregate of consciousness.
These states are accompanied by zest.
Which states are without zest?
Those in the plane without zest: in the sense-sphere, the fine-material sphere, the immaterial sphere, and the unincluded (apariyāpanna).
The aggregate of feeling …pe… the aggregate of consciousness;
rapture, all form, and the unconditioned element—
these phenomena are without rapture.
2.3.2.13.8. The Dyad Associated with Rapture (Pītisahagataduka) Which phenomena are associated with rapture?

Those on the plane of rapture—whether belonging to the sense sphere, the fine-material sphere, or the unincluded (apariyāpanna)—excluding rapture itself: the aggregate of feeling associated with it …pe… the aggregate of consciousness.
These phenomena are accompanied by rapture.
Which phenomena are not accompanied by rapture?
Those that are not on the plane of rapture: those in the sense sphere, the fine-material sphere, the immaterial sphere, and the unincluded (apariyāpanna).
The aggregate of feeling …pe… the aggregate of consciousness;
rapture, all form, and the unconditioned element—
these phenomena are not accompanied by rapture.
2.3.2.13.9. The Pairs Associated with Pleasure (Sukhasahagataduka) Which phenomena are associated with pleasure?

In the plane of pleasure—the sense sphere, the fine-material sphere, and the unincluded (transcendent)—excluding pleasure itself, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness that are associated with it.
These phenomena are accompanied by pleasure.
Which phenomena are not accompanied by pleasure?
Those that are not on the plane of pleasure: those in the sense sphere, the fine-material sphere, the immaterial sphere, and the unincluded (apariyāpanna).
The aggregate of feeling …pe… the aggregate of consciousness;
pleasure, all form, and the unconditioned element—
these phenomena are not accompanied by pleasure.
2.3.2.13.10. The Pair Concerning Accompanied by Equanimity (Upekkhāsahagataduka) Which phenomena are accompanied by equanimity?

Those on the plane of equanimity belonging to the sense sphere, the fine-material sphere, the immaterial sphere, and the unincluded (apariyāpanna), excluding equanimity itself; namely, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness associated with it.
These states are accompanied by equanimity.
Which states are not accompanied by equanimity?

In the plane of equanimity—the sense sphere, the fine-material sphere, and the unincluded—there are the aggregate of feeling …pe… the aggregate of consciousness, equanimity itself, all form, and the unconditioned element.
These phenomena are not accompanied by equanimity.
2.3.2.13.11. The Sensual-Sphere Dyad:
Which phenomena belong to the sensual sphere?
Below, taking the Avīci hell as its limit, and above, taking the Paranimmitavasavatti devas as its limit,
whatever aggregates, elements, and bases are included within this interval,
and whatever form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness there are—
These phenomena belong to the sense sphere.
Which phenomena do not belong to the sense sphere?
Those belonging to the fine-material sphere, those belonging to the immaterial sphere, and those that are unincluded.
These states do not belong to the sense sphere (kāmāvacara).
2.3.2.13.12. The Dyad of the Form Sphere (rūpāvacara-dvika):
Which states belong to the form sphere?
With the Brahma-world as its lower limit and including the Akaniṭṭha devas above,

whatever mental states and mental factors there are within this interval— whether belonging to one who has attained meditative absorption, or to one who has been reborn there, or to one dwelling in happiness in this very life— are included therein.
These phenomena belong to the fine-material sphere.
Which phenomena do not belong to the fine-material sphere?
Those belonging to the sense-sphere, those belonging to the immaterial sphere, and those that are unincluded.
These phenomena do not belong to the fine-material sphere.
2.3.2.13.13. The Pair on the Immaterial Sphere:
Which phenomena belong to the immaterial sphere?
Delimiting below the gods who have reached the base of infinite space, and delimiting above the gods who have reached the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
whatever mental states and mental factors there are within this interval— belonging to this sphere, included within this interval, whether of one who has attained meditative absorption,
or of one who has been reborn there, or of one dwelling in happiness in this very life— [these are the formless aggregates].
These states belong to the formless realm (arūpāvacara).
Which states do not belong to the formless realm?
Those belonging to the sense realm (kāmāvacara), those belonging to the fine-material realm (rūpāvacara), and those that are unconditioned (apariyāpanna).
These phenomena are not of the formless realm.
2.3.2.13.14. The Pair on the Included:
Which phenomena are included?
Tainted wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate states belonging to the sense sphere, the fine-material sphere, and the immaterial sphere— the aggregate of form …pe… the aggregate of consciousness—
these states are included (pariyāpanna).
Which states are not included (apariyāpanna)?
The paths, the fruits of the paths, and the unconditioned element—these phenomena are not included within the realms.
2.3.2.13.15. The Dyad on Leading Outward.
Which phenomena are leading out?
The four paths that are not included within the mundane—
these phenomena are leading out.
Which phenomena are non-emancipating?

With the exception of those [noble] phenomena, all remaining wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena belonging to the sense sphere, the fine-material sphere, the immaterial sphere, and the unincluded [supramundane];
the aggregate of feeling …pe… the aggregate of consciousness; all form; and the unconditioned element.
These phenomena are not leading to liberation.
2.3.2.13.16. The Pair on the Fixed:
Which phenomena are fixed?
The five deeds with immediate retribution, the fixed wrong view, and the four paths not included [within the realms]—
these phenomena are fixed.
Which phenomena are unfixed?

Excluding those states, all remaining wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate states—whether belonging to the sense sphere, the fine-material sphere, the immaterial sphere, or the unincluded (apariyāpanna);
the aggregate of feeling …pe… the aggregate of consciousness; all form, and the unconditioned element—these states are undetermined (aniyata).
2.3.2.13.17. With-Surpassable (Sauttaraduka).
Which phenomena are with-surpassable?

They are the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena associated with the taints (sāsava), belonging to the sense sphere (kāmāvacara), the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), and the immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara).
The aggregate of form …pe… the aggregate of consciousness—
these phenomena are surpassable.
Which phenomena are unsurpassable?
The paths that are not included [within the mundane], the fruits of the paths, and the unconditioned element—these states are unsurpassed.
2.3.2.13.18. The Dyad on Taking Refuge.
Which phenomena are with a basis?
The three unwholesome roots: greed, hatred, and delusion;

the defilements associated with them; the aggregate of feeling associated with them …pe… the aggregate of consciousness associated with them; and the bodily action, verbal action, and mental action originated by them.
These phenomena are with conflict (*saraṇa*).
Which phenomena are without conflict (*araṇa*)?
Wholesome and indeterminate phenomena pertaining to the sense-sphere, the fine-material sphere, the immaterial sphere, and those not included [within the realms]; these are without conflict.
The aggregate of feeling ... [and so on] ... the aggregate of consciousness, all form, and the unconditioned element—these phenomena are without conflict (araṇa).
This is the Abhidhamma dyad.
